Borrowed from Italian trampolino (“springboard”), diminutive of Italian trampolo (“stilt”), from German trampeln (“to trample, stamp”), from Middle High German trampeln. The Germanic word belongs to a family ultimately reconstructed as Proto-West Germanic *trampan (“to step”), from *trampaną (“to step, tramp”), generally regarded as onomatopoeic in origin. A further connection with *drem- (“to run”) has been proposed, but is uncertain.
Compare the parallel borrowings Norwegian Nynorsk trampoline, Danish trampolin, Swedish trampolin, German Trampolin, Dutch trampoline, French trampoline and Spa

18782.etyen:
første (“first”) + mai (“May”) + tog (“parade, procession”), literally “first-of-May parade”.
The first element første is from Old Norse fyrstr (“first”), from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first, foremost”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”). mai is ultimately from Latin Maius (“May”). The final element tog (“parade, procession”) is from Middle Low German toch (“journey, procession; act of pulling”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *teuhaną (“to pull, lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk førstemaitog, fyrstemaitog and Swed

The original phrase appears to be “A man without faith is like a fish without a bicycle”, coined by Charles S. Harris in 1955 and published in a 1958 article in the Swarthmore Phoenix. 1005150.etyen:
From noen (“some”) + -lunde (“manner- or degree-forming suffix”), literally “in some manner”.
The first element is from Old Norse nǫkkurn, the masculine accusative singular of nǫkkurr (“some, any”), earlier nakkvarr, from Proto-Norse. Its origin is traditionally analysed as a contraction of *ni-wait-(ek-)hwarjaʀ (“I do not know who”); reconstructions differ over whether the independent pronoun “I” was present. The negative element continues Proto-Germanic *ne (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né (“not”); the verbal element belongs to Proto-Germanic *witaną (“to know”), ultimately from Proto-I
